title: Cancers Once Diagnosed at 60 Are Now Striking People in Their 30s and 40s, and Researchers Think They Know Why
excerpt: A landmark Nature Medicine study links accelerated biological aging in younger generations to the global surge in early-onset cancers, with implications for how we screen and prevent the disease.
body:
• Cancers diagnosed before age 50 increased 24% worldwide between 1990 and 2019, with people born in the 1990s facing fourfold higher colorectal cancer risk than those born in the 1960s
  • A new Nature Medicine study found that accelerated biological aging — where the body ages faster than its chronological years — is significantly linked to early-onset cancer risk
  • Organ-specific aging patterns matter: older-appearing immune systems were linked to lung cancer, while accelerated fat tissue aging was tied to colorectal cancer
  • Researchers say blood-based biomarkers could identify high-risk individuals years before diagnosis, enabling earlier screening and personalised prevention

The Numbers Are Alarming

Cancer was long considered a disease of aging — the accumulated wear of decades finally catching up. That assumption is breaking down. Diagnoses of cancer in adults under 50 surged 24% globally between 1990 and 2019. In the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia, people born in the 1990s face at least four times the risk of early-onset colorectal cancer compared with those born in the 1960s.

The trend cuts across geography and ethnicity. And until recently, nobody could explain why.

The Biological Aging Connection

A study published in Nature Medicine in June 2026 offers what may be the most compelling explanation yet. Researchers at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis analysed biological aging — measuring how old the body appears versus how old it actually is — across large population cohorts.

Their finding: people born in more recent decades show larger gaps between biological and chronological age. Their bodies, in effect, are aging faster than their parents' and grandparents' bodies did at the same point in life. And the larger that gap, the higher the cancer risk.

"If we can identify younger people with the highest cancer risk when they are still healthy, we can focus on prevention and early-detection strategies for the individuals who will benefit most from early interventions."

— Yin Cao, Washington University School of Medicine

Not All Aging Is Equal

The study went further, identifying organ-specific aging patterns tied to specific cancers. An immune system that appears older than its chronological age was associated with early-onset lung cancer. Fat tissue that has aged prematurely was linked to early-onset colorectal cancer.

This granularity matters. It suggests that cancer risk is not a single switch but a constellation of signals — some detectable through blood tests years before any symptoms appear.

What's Driving Accelerated Aging?

The researchers point to modern environmental and lifestyle factors — though specifics remain under investigation. Ultra-processed diets, sedentary lifestyles, chronic stress, disrupted sleep, and exposure to environmental chemicals are all suspected contributors. The fact that younger birth cohorts show consistently higher biological aging suggests these factors are compounding generationally.

"Our ultimate goal is to decode how modern environments become biologically embedded to drive cancer risk, transforming prevention from broad recommendations to personalised interventions," said Yin Cao, a molecular epidemiologist and associate professor at WashU Medicine.

What This Means for You

The practical implication is straightforward: cancer screening guidelines written for older populations may need to be rethought. Over 60% of cancers diagnosed in adults under 50 are screen-detectable, according to a separate analysis using National Cancer Institute data. Colorectal cancer screening, for instance, was recently lowered to age 45 in the US — but this research suggests that for some individuals, even that may not be early enough.

For the Indian diaspora, the findings carry particular weight. India already faces a rising burden of early-onset cancers, driven by changing diets and urbanisation. South Asians in Western countries are not immune — studies have flagged higher rates of certain cancers in younger South Asian populations compared with their white counterparts. This research reinforces the case for proactive screening and lifestyle intervention, regardless of age.
